solutionSteps: \textnormal{A nonzero branch can leave zero precisely when its escape-time integral is finite. Substitution }u=\ln(1/y)\textnormal{ changes that integral to }\int^{\infty}\frac{\mathrm du}{u^{\alpha_j}(\ln u)^{\beta_j}}.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Duhamel gives the endpoint kernels }h_1(t)=\frac{\sin(1(\frac{\pi}{3}-t))}{1},\quad h_2(t)=\cos(1(\frac{\pi}{3}-t)).

\textnormal{Let }e=(1,0)^{\mathsf T},\quad f_*(t)=(G^{-1}e)^{\mathsf T}(h_1(t),h_2(t))^{\mathsf T}.\textnormal{This forcing satisfies both moments. Any other feasible forcing differs from it by a function orthogonal to both kernels, so Pythagoras proves minimality.}
\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}f_*^2\,\mathrm dt=e^{\mathsf T}G^{-1}e.

\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}f_*^2\,\mathrm dt=e^{\mathsf T}G^{-1}e.

analyticCertificate: Termwise differentiation of the entire series gives the Bessel ODE, its derivative recurrence, and the regular-origin behavior. For order zero the derivative is O(z), and for positive integer order the function is O(z^n); these imply F(0)=0. A positive root and its derivative cannot both vanish by uniqueness for the nonsingular ODE at that point. Existence and ordering of positive Bessel zeros are standard oscillation-theory prerequisites, not asserted as machine proved. All positive zeros exceed two: on (0,2], the defining alternating series has decreasing term magnitudes; for positive integer order its first term strictly exceeds the second, and for order zero at z=2 the first two cancel but the remaining alternating tail is strictly positive. Thus alpha squared exceeds four. Together with the nonzero root derivative, this strictly orders all authored alternatives and certifies their inequivalence; symbolic non-simplification alone is not used as that proof.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Let }X(E)>0\textnormal{ be the inverse of the increasing positive branch of }V.\textnormal{ Energy conservation gives }P(E)=2\sqrt2\int_0^E\frac{X\prime(v)}{\sqrt{E-v}}\,\mathrm dv.

\textnormal{Insert the stated period and integrate its constant and linear terms: }X(E)=\sqrt{2E}\left(1+\frac{2}3E\right).\textnormal{Evaluate at the requested energy.}

For diagonal positive S=diag(s1,s2), the map N to SNS has coordinate factors s1 squared, s2 squared and s1*s2, so its three-dimensional Jacobian is (det S)^3. solutionSteps: \textnormal{For any smooth u, the cofactor identity is }\nabla\cdot\left((\operatorname{cof}D^2u)\nabla u\right)=2\det D^2u.

\textnormal{On the unit circle u vanishes. With outward normal n and unit tangent tau, twice differentiating the boundary trace gives }\tau^{\mathsf T}D^2u\,\tau=u_n.\textnormal{Therefore the outward cofactor flux is }u_n^2.

\textnormal{For this polynomial, }u_n=-2\left[1+1\cos(2\theta)\right].\textnormal{The divergence theorem reduces the integral to }\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}4\left[1+1\cos(2\theta)\right]^2\,\mathrm d\theta.
\textnormal{The cosine mean is zero and its squared integral is pi.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{For any smooth u, the cofactor identity is }\nabla\cdot\left((\operatorname{cof}D^2u)\nabla u\right)=2\det D^2u.

\textnormal{On the unit circle u vanishes. With outward normal n and unit tangent tau, twice differentiating the boundary trace gives }\tau^{\mathsf T}D^2u\,\tau=u_n.\textnormal{Therefore the outward cofactor flux is }u_n^2.

\textnormal{For this polynomial, }u_n=-2\left[1+1\cos(5\theta)\right].\textnormal{The divergence theorem reduces the integral to }\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}4\left[1+1\cos(5\theta)\right]^2\,\mathrm d\theta.
\textnormal{The cosine mean is zero and its squared integral is pi.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{For any smooth u, the cofactor identity is }\nabla\cdot\left((\operatorname{cof}D^2u)\nabla u\right)=2\det D^2u.

\textnormal{On the unit circle u vanishes. With outward normal n and unit tangent tau, twice differentiating the boundary trace gives }\tau^{\mathsf T}D^2u\,\tau=u_n.\textnormal{Therefore the outward cofactor flux is }u_n^2.

\textnormal{For this polynomial, }u_n=-2\left[1+2\cos(2\theta)\right].\textnormal{The divergence theorem reduces the integral to }\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}4\left[1+2\cos(2\theta)\right]^2\,\mathrm d\theta.
\textnormal{The cosine mean is zero and its squared integral is pi.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{For any smooth u, the cofactor identity is }\nabla\cdot\left((\operatorname{cof}D^2u)\nabla u\right)=2\det D^2u.

\textnormal{On the unit circle u vanishes. With outward normal n and unit tangent tau, twice differentiating the boundary trace gives }\tau^{\mathsf T}D^2u\,\tau=u_n.\textnormal{Therefore the outward cofactor flux is }u_n^2.

\textnormal{For this polynomial, }u_n=-2\left[1+2\cos(5\theta)\right].\textnormal{The divergence theorem reduces the integral to }\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}4\left[1+2\cos(5\theta)\right]^2\,\mathrm d\theta.
\textnormal{The cosine mean is zero and its squared integral is pi.}
12 \pi

solutionSteps: \textnormal{For any smooth u, the cofactor identity is }\nabla\cdot\left((\operatorname{cof}D^2u)\nabla u\right)=2\det D^2u.

\textnormal{On the unit circle u vanishes. With outward normal n and unit tangent tau, twice differentiating the boundary trace gives }\tau^{\mathsf T}D^2u\,\tau=u_n.\textnormal{Therefore the outward cofactor flux is }u_n^2.

\textnormal{For this polynomial, }u_n=-2\left[1+2\cos(6\theta)\right].\textnormal{The divergence theorem reduces the integral to }\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}4\left[1+2\cos(6\theta)\right]^2\,\mathrm d\theta.
\textnormal{The cosine mean is zero and its squared integral is pi.}

The quartic terms are convex and coercive, so the global minimizer is unique. Its stationarity equation is }Az+z^{\circ3}=t v,\quad v=\left[\begin{matrix}1\\0\end{matrix}\right].

\textnormal{The envelope identity is }m\prime(t)=-v^{\mathsf T}z(t).\textnormal{Since A is symmetric, }-v^{\mathsf T}r=w^{\mathsf T}w^{\circ3}=w_1^4+w_2^4.
\textnormal{Integrate the cubic coefficient of the derivative, or differentiate it three times, to obtain }m^{(4)}(0)=6(w_1^4+w_2^4).

\textnormal{The implicit function theorem and odd symmetry give }z(t)=t w+t^3r+O(t^5),\quad w=A^{-1}v=\left[\begin{matrix}\frac{2}{5}\\\frac{1}{5}\end{matrix}\right],\quad r=-A^{-1}w^{\circ3}.
\textnormal{The envelope identity is }m\prime(t)=-v^{\mathsf T}z(t).\textnormal{Since A is symmetric, }-v^{\mathsf T}r=w^{\mathsf T}w^{\circ3}=w_1^4+w_2^4.
\textnormal{Integrate the cubic coefficient of the derivative, or differentiate it three times, to obtain }m^{(4)}(0)=6(w_1^4+w_2^4).

solutionSteps: \textnormal{For every nonnegative integer }k,\textnormal{ let }P_k\textnormal{ be the monic degree-k solution of the analogous equation. Comparing coefficients gives existence and uniqueness, with }P_0=1,\quad P_1=x.

\textnormal{Differentiating its differential equation shows that the derivative divided by k is the previous monic solution. Combining that identity with the equation at degree k minus one gives }P_k\prime=kP_{k-1},\qquad P_k=xP_{k-1}-\frac{k-1}{2}P_{k-2}.
\textnormal{No root can be repeated: simultaneous zero value and derivative would force the entire differential-equation solution to vanish. Define the inter-degree product over all roots of }P_k.
R_k=\prod_{P_k(r)=0}P_{k-1}(r),\qquad R_1=1.

\textnormal{Reverse the products over the two root sets. The sign is positive because k times k minus one is even. At a root of the previous polynomial, the three-term recurrence removes its first term.}
R_k=\prod_{P_{k-1}(u)=0}P_k(u)=\left(-\frac{k-1}{2}\right)^{k-1}R_{k-1}.
\textnormal{The derivative product counts each pair difference in both orientations, whereas the requested discriminant counts its square once.}
\prod_{i<j}(r_i-r_j)^2=2^{-k(k-1)/2}\prod_{j=1}^{k}j^j\quad\textnormal{at }k=8.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{For every nonnegative integer }k,\textnormal{ let }P_k\textnormal{ be the monic degree-k solution of the analogous equation. Comparing coefficients gives existence and uniqueness, with }P_0=1,\quad P_1=x.

\textnormal{Differentiating its differential equation shows that the derivative divided by k is the previous monic solution. Combining that identity with the equation at degree k minus one gives }P_k\prime=kP_{k-1},\qquad P_k=xP_{k-1}-\frac{k-1}{2}P_{k-2}.
\textnormal{No root can be repeated: simultaneous zero value and derivative would force the entire differential-equation solution to vanish. Define the inter-degree product over all roots of }P_k.
R_k=\prod_{P_k(r)=0}P_{k-1}(r),\qquad R_1=1.

\textnormal{Reverse the products over the two root sets. The sign is positive because k times k minus one is even. At a root of the previous polynomial, the three-term recurrence removes its first term.}
R_k=\prod_{P_{k-1}(u)=0}P_k(u)=\left(-\frac{k-1}{2}\right)^{k-1}R_{k-1}.
\textnormal{The derivative product counts each pair difference in both orientations, whereas the requested discriminant counts its square once.}
\prod_{i<j}(r_i-r_j)^2=2^{-k(k-1)/2}\prod_{j=1}^{k}j^j\quad\textnormal{at }k=15.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Write H for the Hessian and cof H for its cofactor matrix. Commuting third derivatives gives the divergence identity }\nabla\cdot\bigl((\operatorname{cof}H)\nabla u\bigr)=2\det H.

\textnormal{On the boundary the tangential derivative vanishes, so the gradient equals its normal component times the outward unit normal. Twice differentiating the zero boundary trace along the unit circle gives }\tau^{\mathsf T}H\tau=u_n,\qquad n^{\mathsf T}(\operatorname{cof}H)\nabla u=u_n^2.
\textnormal{The divergence theorem therefore removes all unspecified interior values.}
\iint_D\det H\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy=\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}u_n(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)^2\,\mathrm d\theta.
\textnormal{The constant Fourier mode contributes two pi, each squared nonconstant mode contributes pi, and all mixed integrals vanish.}
\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}u_n^2\,\mathrm d\theta=\pi\left[1+\frac12\left(\frac14+\frac{1}{4}\right)\right].
\textnormal{The prescribed class is nonempty: in polar coordinates the following expression is a smooth polynomial in the Cartesian coordinates and has exactly the required boundary data.}
u_0(r,\theta)=\frac{r^2-1}{2}\left(1+\frac12r^{1}\cos(1\theta)+\frac{1}{2}r^{2}\sin(2\theta)\right).

\textnormal{The divergence theorem therefore removes all unspecified interior values.}
\iint_D\det H\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy=\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}u_n(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)^2\,\mathrm d\theta.
\textnormal{The constant Fourier mode contributes two pi, each squared nonconstant mode contributes pi, and all mixed integrals vanish.}
\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}u_n^2\,\mathrm d\theta=\pi\left[1+\frac12\left(\frac14+\frac{1}{9}\right)\right].

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Write H for the Hessian and cof H for its cofactor matrix. Commuting third derivatives gives the divergence identity }\nabla\cdot\bigl((\operatorname{cof}H)\nabla u\bigr)=2\det H.

\textnormal{On the boundary the tangential derivative vanishes, so the gradient equals its normal component times the outward unit normal. Twice differentiating the zero boundary trace along the unit circle gives }\tau^{\mathsf T}H\tau=u_n,\qquad n^{\mathsf T}(\operatorname{cof}H)\nabla u=u_n^2.
\textnormal{The divergence theorem therefore removes all unspecified interior values.}
\iint_D\det H\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy=\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}u_n(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)^2\,\mathrm d\theta.
\textnormal{The constant Fourier mode contributes two pi, each squared nonconstant mode contributes pi, and all mixed integrals vanish.}
\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}u_n^2\,\mathrm d\theta=\pi\left[1+\frac12\left(\frac14+\frac{1}{64}\right)\right].
\textnormal{The prescribed class is nonempty: in polar coordinates the following expression is a smooth polynomial in the Cartesian coordinates and has exactly the required boundary data.}
u_0(r,\theta)=\frac{r^2-1}{2}\left(1+\frac12r^{7}\cos(7\theta)+\frac{1}{8}r^{8}\sin(8\theta)\right).

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Put the powers of each point in a row of the Vandermonde matrix. Its determinant is the product of pairwise differences.}
V_{jk}=z_j^{k-1}\quad(1\le j,k\le5),\qquad|\det V|^2=\prod_{i<j}|z_i-z_j|^2.
\textnormal{Each row has squared Euclidean norm at most the number of columns. Hadamard inequality bounds a determinant by the product of row norms.}

\textnormal{Take all distinct roots of unity of this order. Every row then has the maximal norm, and distinct rows are orthogonal because their inner product is a geometric sum with nontrivial unit ratio.}
z_j=e^{2\pi i(j-1)/5},\qquad\sum_{k=0}^{4}(z_j\overline{z_\ell})^k=0\quad(j\ne\ell).
\textnormal{Thus equality in Hadamard is attained, proving that the upper bound is the requested maximum. Here i is the imaginary unit and the bar denotes complex conjugation.}
